newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS - Rhone-Poulenc clings to forecast post recall.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Rhone-Poulenc clings to forecast post recall.

text.p: French chemical and pharmaceuticals group Rhone-Poulenc SA reported a 6.5 percent rise in first quarter net income on Wednesday which showed the scars of a costly product recall.
The figures were in line with expectations but the market welcomed the fact that the company was clinging to its forecast of a 20 percent 1997 profit increase.
Around 1000 GMT, Rhone shares were up 5.64 percent at 198.50 francs after a 9.1 percent opening jump.

Rhone-Poulenc said in a statement the increase in first quarter net income would have been nearly 30 percent but for the recall of a blood plasma product by the Centeon joint-venture in the United States between Rhone-Poulenc Rorer and Germany's Hoechst.
The first quarter net income rose to 674 million francs ($115.9 million) from 633 million on 2.2 percent higher sales at 21.6 billion francs.
On a comparable basis, taking account of sales and acquisitions, sales would have been up 6.3 percent.
Chairman and chief executive Jean-Rene Fourtou said that new products were fuelling earnings, which made him confident of the company's profit aim despite Centeon.
"The new products launched in the life sciences businesses are contributing more and more significantly to the group's results," he said.

"This is why we are maintaining our objective of increasing earnings per shares in 1997 by 20 percent, excluding exceptional items, an objective which is becoming more difficult because of the effect of Centeon," he added.
Such new products are the Taxotere anti-cancer drug, the Nasacort asthma drug, the Rilutek medicament for the treatment of moto-neuron diseases and the Tripedia vaccine.

Operating income showed a 18.8 percent rise on a comparable basis to two billion francs. This reflected a big rise in pharmaceuticals and a small improvement and Fibers and Polymers as well as in animal health while the chemicals division showed a decline.
The chemicals division remained influenced by continued depressed titanium dioxide markets and the increased cost of some raw materials.
Fibres and polymers showed an increase despite a depressed polyester market, especially in Brazil.

A company spokeswoman said manufacturing at Centeon had not resumed but was expected to do so soon with sales and distribution resuming in the second quarter of 1997. "Generally, the impact has been worse than we thought at the end of last year," she said.
Centeon LCC in October recalled its Albumin and Plasma Plex products as a precaution against bacterial infection after some vials of the products had shown cracks.
In January, Rhone-Poulenc said that the Centeon problems had cost 0.64 francs on the 1996 earnings per share figure, which was up 25.8 percent to 8.44 francs.
Financial analysts said the figures were in line with expectations and they were keeping their full-year estimates.
"The figures were as we expected and it is good to see that they are on track to the 1997 target," said analyst Paul Satchell of Paribas in London.

"I had a strong buy out and I maintain that strong buy," he said, adding the only point of disappointment was in animal and plant health where operating income was affected by launch costs and the start-up costs of a plant.
A Paris-based analyst said that the company statement on still aiming for a 20 percent rise in earnings per share in 1997 was encouraging.
"Centeon is weighing on the results for longer than had been believed but they are nevertheless maintaining the forecast of a 20 percent rise," the analyst said.
The company profit forecast was before exceptional items and should therefore not be influenced by the higher asset sales Rhone plans to make in 1997.
Chairman Fourtou told the general meeting earlier this month that the company believed it could make five billion francs in asset sales instead of the three billion it had previously pencilled in.

According to Edinburg Financial Publishers, financial analysts are expecting a 1997 earnings per share for Rhone-Poulenc of 11.10 francs, rising to 14.20 francs in 1998. The 1996 figure was 8.44 francs.

According to Jacques Chahine Finance, a Paris based research bureau which collates analysts' forecasts, the market is expecting Rhone to post a earnings per share figure of 11.21 francs in 1997 and 13.63 franc in 1998.
